claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable single-phase solid solution.
Thermal exposure or simulated service aging induces decomposition of the metastable solid solution.
The decomposition proceeds by nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds.
The precipitated intermetallic compounds are Mg-rich and may also be Ti-rich.
Intermetallic compounds preferentially form along grain boundaries and within grains.
Local compositional fluctuations promote intermetallic phase formation from the metastable matrix.
Energetically favorable nucleation sites promote intermetallic phase formation from the metastable matrix.
Intermetallic precipitation locally depletes critical alloying elements.
Intermetallic evolution alters the integrity, formation, or connectivity of the protective oxide scale.
Protective oxide-scale integrity controls corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Retention or loss of corrosion and oxidation resistance depends on the degree and morphology of intermetallic precipitation.
Aged samples will exhibit a distinct distribution of intermetallic compounds relative to the initial metastable state.
The distribution of intermetallic compounds in aged samples will correlate with reduced or otherwise modified corrosion and oxidation performance.
Suppressing intermetallic formation will preserve more uniform corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The initial metastable solid-solution state has uniform corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The proposed mechanism applies under service temperatures and exposure durations sufficient to produce significant intermetallic precipitation while oxidation or corrosive attack occurs.
